feedback: Karthik? Haan, he is good. Very sincere boy. Comes on time, leaves on time — actually he stays late most days, I don't ask him to. He's always on the floor. He's not one of those people who sits in the office and sends emails. He's hands-on. What does he do? He helps me with production tracking. Earlier I used to maintain everything in my head — how many pieces came off each machine, what's the rejection rate, what's pending for dispatch. Now Karthik maintains a sheet. Every evening he updates it and sends it to me on WhatsApp. Very useful. I look at it every morning before the shift meeting. He also handles a lot of the coordination. When we have quality complaints from Tier 1 — they send an email, sometimes call directly — Karthik takes the first call. He notes down the complaint, talks to the QC team, and gives me a summary. Earlier I used to handle all of this myself. Big relief. The new drum brake line — he's been involved from the beginning. He helped set up the machine layout. He did a study on cycle times and suggested we move the deburring station closer to the CNC machines. Good idea. We did it. Saved maybe 10 minutes per batch in material handling. Any complaints? No, not really. Sometimes he asks too many questions — like he wants to understand everything before doing it. Sometimes in a factory you just need to do it and learn by doing. But this is a minor thing. One thing — he doesn't really push back. If I tell him to do something, he does it. Even if it's not the best way. I wish he would tell me sometimes, 'Sir, I think we should do it differently.' But maybe he's still new. He'll get there. Overall I'm happy. He's become part of the team. The workers on the floor know him. He speaks to them in Marathi — that helps. If you asked them, they would say he's one of us.

Meena. Look, she is smart. No doubt. She understands things quickly. But I have some concerns. She spends too much time on her laptop. In a garment factory, the action is on the floor — cutting, stitching, finishing, packing. If you're not on the floor, you're not seeing what's happening. She made some Excel sheets. One is an order tracker — which order is at which stage. Another one tracks rejection percentages by line. She found that Line 3 has 14% rejection compared to 6% average on the other lines. Nobody had quantified this before. But here's my problem — the data is correct but the people on the floor already know. She is telling us what we already know, just in Excel format. She also wrote an SOP for the cutting section. It's well-written. But nobody uses it. She pinned it on the wall. It's still there. Nobody reads it. On the positive side — she started tracking which orders are at risk of missing the ship date and sending me a daily email by 11 AM. Before this, I would find out about delays at 4 PM. Now I know by 11 AM and can push. Two weeks ago we saved a shipment to Decathlon because of this. That was good. My worry is that she's building things in Excel that nobody asked for and nobody uses. I need someone who solves problems on the floor. Is she failing? No. She's trying. She's just not connecting her work to what actually matters here. If she learns to do that, she could be very good.

My right hand. Don't know how we managed before him. He handles all my meetings now, manages my schedule, takes calls from vendors, resolves everything. He's like the second founder. He does my planning work, runs the production reports, coordinates with the quality team. Frankly, he's absorbed so much of my workload that I'm worried what happens if he leaves. The sales are up because he manages client relationships now. He's a fantastic person, very dedicated. Always available. When he's on the floor or in the office, things just work smoothly. He's learned the business faster than anyone I've seen. Everything flows through him. The energy and enthusiasm he brings is remarkable. He's become essential to operations. If he takes a week off, we're stuck.

She's been tracking production bottlenecks and identified that our assembly line loses 3 hours daily during shift changes. She built a detailed analysis showing exactly where the gaps are. Then she created a new workflow and implemented it with the team. Defects are down 15%. Quality improved noticeably. She also trained the floor team on the new process, and they adopted it within two weeks. She comes up with ideas constantly — last week she suggested a simpler packaging approach and ran a small test. It worked. Now we're evaluating rolling it out company-wide. She's not just executing tasks. She's thinking about the business, spotting patterns, testing solutions, and driving real improvements. The team respects her work because they see the results.
